catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-1-q1.explanation: A - golden Golden age is a collocation that means ‘the best time or period in history of something’. Other adjectives do not make any collocation.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-1-q2.explanation: D - make Same as before, to make a parachute jump is an accepted collocation.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-1-q3.explanation: B - height The answer is height of fame.Even though top of fame sounds acceptable, the first option is a much more widely used way of saying this.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-1-q4.explanation: A - covering B — stretching means the distance, but it wouldn’t say whether she has travelled it or not. C — crossing doesn’t collocate well with

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-1-q5.explanation: C - hailed Because of preposition ‘as’ following the gap we should be using this word (to hail as). Rest of the words aren’t used with ‘as’ in this context.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-1-q6.explanation: A - cut ‘To cut short’ means ‘to stop prematurely, before its time’. The context then goes about how the woman tragically died in an air accident. ‘To bring up short’ means to stop somebody abruptly, but it would need an extra preposition ‘up’ here.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-1-q7.explanation: B - suffered Know the difference between ‘suffer’ and ‘suffer from’. The first one usually happens instantly (like a trauma), while the second is more continuous (‘suffer from cancer’).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-1-q8.explanation: D - same ‘Never the same’ means that she never recovered. Other options do not collocate with definite article.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-2-q9.explanation: It is important to understand why it is ‘happened to’ and not ‘happened with’. Basically, ‘happened with’ is an unusual case, found in phrases like ‘what’s wrong with you?’ or ‘what happened between you two?’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-2-q10.explanation: howHe came to realize the extent of his boredom — how bored he became.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-2-q11.explanation: Meaning is the same as ‘to be sporty’, but instead of infinitive, we use gerund being.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-2-q12.explanation: Make sure not to use an apostrophe (it’s). First of all, that would mean you are using two words instead of one (it is) and second, that would be the wrong choice.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-2-q13.explanation: Anything but here means ‘definitely not’. The following sentence proves that triathlons are very exciting and offer a number of fun activities, such as running or cycling.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-2-q14.explanation: ‘To move away from’ means to stop doing something and shift your attention elsewhere.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-2-q16.explanation: ‘So on’ = and something similar, something in the same fashion.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-3-q17.explanation: nominationNominating form would be wrong as it would imply that it is the form that nominates something. Nomination form on the other hand, is used for nominations.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-3-q18.explanation: receiptReceipt here means ‘the act of receiving something’. ‘Receival’ doesn’t fit here as it isn’t a word, or a word that is commonly used or known. ‘Receiving’ can’t be used because it can’t be used with ‘of’ preposition. You are generally discourages to use -ing to form noun in CAE Reading and Use of English Part 3.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-3-q19.explanation: dinersDiner here means a person who attends a restaurant or any other food outlet. Note that a diner can also mean a small restaurant, usually one by the road (mostly used in AmE).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-3-q21.explanation: contestedContested means involving strong competition among a number of people because it is desirable. Do not confuse it with ‘contestable’ which means ‘rising a lot of doubts and arguments about’. Nothing like that is implied by the context.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-3-q22.explanation: deadlineDeadline is the time limit for something, in this case for sending your application.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-3-q23.explanation: unannouncedIt is implied that the visits are going to be anonymous and the restaurant owners won’t know anything about it — these visits will be unannounced.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-3-q24.explanation: prestigiousMind the spelling of this word, remember that any typos are counted as wrong answer even if you got the word right.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-4-q25.explanation: a while before/until/till I fullyA while = some time. E.g.: ‘I haven’t seen you for a while!’ = I haven’t seen you for some time.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-4-q26.explanation: isn’t /is not worth arguing aboutNot point doing something = not worth doing something. Use ‘argue’ with ‘about’ here or it will be counted as a mistake.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-4-q27.explanation: there be any/a delayTo make it easier to understand, just replace ‘should’ with ‘if’ (in your head, not on the paper!). Note that this is a conditional inversion.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-4-q28.explanation: have anything in common withTo have something in common = to have similarities. If there are no similarities, then there is nothing in common. If the beginning of sentence went ‘The two situations ___’ then you could have used ‘have nothing in common’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-4-q29.explanation: my amazement, nothing wentTo my amazement = I was amazed. To have problems = to go wrong. The comma here is optional.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-4-q30.answer: wouldn’t/would not dream of doing any
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-4-q30.explanation: wouldn’t/would not dream of doing anyTo dream of something has several meanings, one of them is ‘to have no intention to do something at all’ or ‘to think of something that is unlikely to take place’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-5-q31.explanation: B Answers A and C aren’t mentioned in the text. AnswerD is too general and is vaguely implied, but not as strongly as B.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-5-q32.explanation: CThird and fourth sentences of second paragraph explain how people motivate themselves to perform better if they see the outcome and impact of their good work on the business as a whole. A and D are not mentioned. Answer B is unrelated to the information in the text, even though the ‘box-ticking’ phrase is used.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-5-q33.explanation: DThe number of clients seen each day wasn’t the ultimate goal of the company, but for the employees it was made as the most important aspect of their job (sentence ‘The sales people obviously …’). Other answers are either not mentioned in the text or unrelated to the question.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-5-q34.explanation: BTo foresee the consequences here mean to see the results of their actions beforehand, in advance. The products got inadequate testing because of lack of time and thus proved to be of poor quality.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-5-q35.explanation: AThe text gives an example how employees of that company were betrayed by senior management in the past and therefore they now have doubts about similar programmes that are introduced. Answer C states it from employees’ perspective, but it isn’t true. Other answers are not mentioned.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-5-q36.explanation: BA self-contained exercise here is treated as a formality rather than as a genuine attempt to change management practice. Last two sentences confirm this attitude of senior management. They get back to their old ways.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-6-q37.explanation: DSecond sentence of Paragraph A states that the studies tend to over-complicate the phenomenon of pop-culture which itself is simple. First sentence of Paragraph D states the same idea in a slightly different way.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-6-q38.explanation: BSpeaker from Paragraph B believes that the whole pop-culture thing is being forced on people by corporations (sentence two: ‘… imposed from on high’) while all other speakers believe that the culture appears by natural means.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-6-q39.explanation: ASpeaker B states that what people buy and consume ‘speaks volumes’ about the culture — meaning that you can tell a lot about it by their consuming. Speaker A in the first sentence says that the phenomenon of pop-culture ‘…is key to the understanding of any modern society.’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-6-q40.explanation: DSpeaker D is convinced that pop-culture can have negative impact on the young people. In the middle of the paragraph he states: ‘…popular culture can have undue influence, encouraging them to acquire unrealistic ideas …therefore potentially having a damaging effect…’. Other speakers hold it that pop-culture provides younger generations with sense of comfort and belonging.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-7-q41.explanation: FThe paragraph begins with ‘They do so …’ referring to the works mentioned in the end of previous paragraph. The paragraph ends with the description of a dark wood in moonlight shine, which matches the beginning of next paragraph, talking about monochrome pictures.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-7-q42.explanation: A‘Claustrophobic and joyless’ stays even when he uses strong colours (by strong here they mean something other that white, black and grey).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-7-q43.explanation: EThe preceding paragraph asks a question on how artist’s talent would have developed if he were to stay in England. The beginning of Paragraph E gives a probable answer to that. It ends with him having to leave the country, and the next paragraph talks about his visit to Greece.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-7-q44.explanation: GAt the end of the previous paragraph artist’s transformation is mentioned, and this topic is developed in Paragraph G. His pictures are no longer grim and devoid of colour, they become vivid.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-7-q45.explanation: CEnding of Paragraph C mentions that Craxton stopped experimenting and developing his art, and the following paragraph expands on that topic: ‘But if there is little exploration or discovery in Craxton’s later work …’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-7-q46.explanation: BHe mentions feeling like an emigre (a political emigrant) in London, and this notion is continued in the paragraph after.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-8-q47.explanation: The first sentence talks about ‘recent rise’ from few to many specimens, and then in the middle of the paragraph they talk of a ‘reintroduction scheme’ inspired by this success.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-8-q48.explanation: The last sentence talks of a ‘resilience of a small bird’. Resilience here means ‘being able to recover quickly and overcome hardships easily’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-8-q49.explanation: ARoyal Society for the Protection of Birds poll suggests that it is one of the most popular birds along with two other specimens mentioned in sentence two of Paragraph A.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-8-q50.explanation: BTwo winters in 1961 and 1962 drastically reduced the population of this bird, according to the middle of Paragraph B.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-8-q51.explanation: The first sentence of the paragraph states that even the most convinced admirers of this bird confess that it looks rather ‘drab’ — or dull, shabby and not arousing any interest.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-8-q52.explanation: The second part of Paragraph B talks about ‘protective instincts’ for these defenseless birds, yet strangely it manages to restore its population.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-8-q53.explanation: The middle of the third paragraph goes: ‘… the pace of increase agonizingly slow’, implying that a faster pace of reintroduction would have been more than welcome.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-8-q54.explanation: CLast sentence of Paragraph C states that there are reasons to believe the rate of breeding is going to continue its increase.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-8-q55.explanation: The second part of Paragraph B talks about ‘intensive management and protection of England’s lowland heath’ that ensured an increased breeding rate of the rare bird.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test3-part-8-q56.explanation: The last sentence of the fourth paragraph states that these birds ‘are often birds of large gardens’ and other buildings, meaning that they can still be seen around frequently.
